title: Ablation: max-length and batching profiles for QA promptset (Aug 2025)
content:
Purpose:
This is a working ablation report that explores latency/cost/quality tradeoffs for a representative QA promptset during model onboarding. The goal is to identify conservative, medium, and aggressive serving profiles (batching + max_length cap + prefix cache policy) that maintain >=98% of baseline answer F1 while reducing per-request cost and improving throughput. This doc captures experiment design, raw observations, anomalous runs, and recommended profiles for the next rollout stage.

Key constraints and decisions made up-front:
- Target workload: web QA assistant with average user prompt length ~24 tokens and typical reference answer length ~48 tokens (source: sampled traffic proxy).
- Baseline model: rwi-open-large-v2 (fp16), baseline serving config uses continuous batching with max_batch_size=64, no prefix cache, max_tokens cap unset (full decode), no quantization.
- Evaluation metrics:
  - Quality: F1 (span overlap) and ROUGE-L on held-out annotated QA promptset (n=1,200).
  - Latency: p50 and p95 generation latency measured end-to-end (ms).
  - Cost proxy: GPU-token cost estimate computed as token_count * token_cost_per_gpu (derived from infra billing); reported as normalized cost per 1k QTokens.
  - Throughput: tokens/sec and requests/sec under steady-state simulated arrival.

Experiment matrix (high-level):
- Max-length caps: {64, 128, 256} (max decode length including prompt).
- Batching profiles: 
  A) conservative: max_batch_size=8, batch_timeout=6ms
  B) balanced: max_batch_size=32, batch_timeout=12ms
  C) aggressive: max_batch_size=96, batch_timeout=25ms (forced larger batches)
- Caching: none | prefix-only (cache embeddings + KV up to 32 tokens) | full prefix (cache up to 128 prompt tokens).
- Each run: 3 warmup minutes + 10-minute steady evaluation at 50 rps synthetic trace (Poisson), repeated twice.

Promptset notes:
- Promptset is an onboarding QA collection assembled from three product templates: short-fact, multi-sentence context, and follow-up clarification pairs. Composition: 40% short-fact, 45% multi-context, 15% follow-up.
- Prompts include noise tokens (system instructions and tool metadata) that inflate prompt length by ~3 tokens on average; experiments include raw prompt tokens in max-length accounting.

Observed highlights (condensed):
1) Quality vs max-length
- Moving cap from unset -> 256: negligible change in F1 (median delta -0.2%); for long-context examples (top 5% longest references) there is a modest -0.8% F1 loss.
- Cap at 128: mean F1 delta -0.6%, worst-case -2.1% on long-context subset.
- Cap at 64: visible drop in ROUGE-L and F1 (-3.4% mean, -7% worst-case).
Interpretation: 128 is a reasonable conservative cap for this QA set; 64 is too aggressive for multi-context questions.

2) Batching tradeoffs
- Conservative (8): p50 latency similar to baseline (small variance), cost per request increases because smaller batches underutilize GPU. p95 improved for single-request latency-sensitive workload.
- Balanced (32): sweet spot for p50/p95 and throughput: p50 reduced 18% vs baseline, p95 increased slightly (5%) likely due to queueing effects for worst-case items. Cost per 1k tokens reduced ~22% because of amortized kernel overhead.
- Aggressive (96): highest throughput and lowest normalized token cost (approx -34% vs baseline), but p95 latency regresses significantly (+60%) and observed tail quality regressions on some concurrency patterns (see anomalies).

3) Caching impact
- Prefix-only (32 tokens): for short-context prompts saw ~12% latency reduction and ~10% cost reduction. Effects are marginal for multi-context prompts where prompt differences exceed cache window.
- Full prefix (128 tokens): larger gains for the multi-context bucket (up to 18% cost saved), but cache eviction churn under aggressive batching caused occasional KV inconsistencies in our runtime snapshot (investigate further).

4) Notable anomalies and runtime observations
- Under aggressive batching + full prefix caching, we observed non-deterministic tail-quality degradations on 0.6% of requests where decoded spans were truncated or repeated. Hypothesis: kernel scheduling + KV eviction race. Reproducible with a synthetic trace that mixes long-context and short-context requests at high concurrency.
- One run on 2025-08-07 showed a spike in p95 (x2 baseline) correlated with a background node GC on a TPU-affine instance; flagged infra ticket (JIRA-OPS-4312).

Quantitative snapshot (median across runs) – representative numbers:
- Baseline (no cap, batch64, no cache): p50 210ms, p95 730ms, F1 0.874, norm_cost_per_1k_tokens = 1.00
- Profile Conservative (cap128, batch8, prefix-only32): p50 198ms, p95 560ms, F1 0.870, cost 1.10
- Profile Balanced (cap128, batch32, prefix-only32): p50 172ms, p95 765ms, F1 0.869, cost 0.78
- Profile Aggressive (cap256, batch96, full-prefix128): p50 130ms, p95 1,160ms, F1 0.855, cost 0.66
Notes on that table: Balanced reduces cost substantially while preserving ~99.4% of baseline F1. Aggressive yields the largest cost savings but fails SLO on p95 and has measurable quality drop. Conservative preserves tail but increases cost slightly.

Recommendations for onboarding rollout (next 2 phases):
- Phase A (canary): adopt Balanced profile (cap=128, batch=32, prefix cache 32) for 10% of traffic on Dedicated clusters. Monitor p95 and quality on the product promptset with alerts: F1 drop >1.5% or p95 >900ms should trigger rollback.
- Phase B (gradual ramp): if canary stable after 72h, expand to 50% traffic and enable opportunistic cache warming policies. Run a focused synthetic trace to reproduce the aggressive-batch KV race and mitigate kernel scheduling mismatch.
- Do NOT adopt Aggressive profile for production until we fix KV eviction race and demonstrate stable tail latencies under mixed workloads.

Operational action items (owners):
- Aakash: reproduce KV eviction race on test harness and file internal bug with clear repro steps (due 2025-08-15).
- Maya: implement canary dashboard tiles (p50/p95 by profile, quality by prompt slice) and set alert thresholds (due 2025-08-18).
- Ethan: run nightly synthetic stress runs that mix short/long contexts to validate tail behavior for batch sizes 32/96 (start 2025-08-13).
- Sofia: prepare customer-facing one-pager with suggested profiles and expected tradeoffs for CS review (draft due 2025-08-19).

Appendix: experiment reproducibility notes
- All experiments tracked via the onboarding-evals repo. Run id patterns: onboarding-qa-YYYYMMDD-HHMM.
- Docker image: rwi/runtime:v20250801-candidate; infra config pinned to nvidia-a100-80gb; same image used across runs.
- Evaluation harness: scripts/eval/qa_batch_ablation.py; parameters included in linked_artifacts PR.
- Raw CSV outputs for the runs are uploaded to GCS path: gs://redwood-evals/onboarding/qa/aug2025/ (see linked_artifacts).

Unanswered questions / follow-ups:
- Can we design a dynamic batching policy that adapts max_batch_size based on prompt-length histogram to avoid worst-case tail regressions? (research task)
- What are concrete kernel-level mitigations for observed KV eviction race? (infra + runtime collaboration)
- Should we expose a "latency-first" vs "cost-first" preset to customers with clear SLO guidance?

Status: in_review. This doc intentionally contains rough numbers and operational notes; will convert to a polished brief after canary results and bug triage.
